en: The national flower, Sampaguita, releases its strongest fragrance at night to attract sphinx moths for pollination.
The Philippine eagle requires at least thirty square kilometers of old-growth forest to hunt and nest successfully.
The national tree, Narra, exhibits nyctinasty, meaning its compound leaves fold downward at night and during rain.
The Ifugao rice terraces utilize a gravity-fed irrigation system where water flows naturally from mountain forests down to paddies.
The Mindoro tamaraw, a symbol of the province, has hooves adapted to walk on steep, muddy mountain slopes.
The South Sea pearl, our national gem, forms when a giant oyster secretes nacre around an irritating particle.
Taal Volcano in Batangas is a unique geological feature consisting of an active crater inside a lake-filled caldera.
Scientist Ramon Barba discovered that spraying mango trees with potassium nitrate induces them to flower out of season.
The Mangyan people of Mindoro traditionally carve their ancient scripts onto the thick internodes of local bamboo species.
The carabao wallows in mud to regulate its body temperature because it lacks sufficient functional sweat glands.
The anahaw palm, our national leaf, features large, circular, fan-like leaves that naturally repel water during heavy rains.
Baguio’s Panagbenga Festival celebrates the blooming of local flowers that thrive in the city's cool, high-altitude climate.
